title: Instrument ranges and fingering: voice, tenor sax, piano
summary: He compares ranges and fingering of tenor sax and baritone with the piano, which demands both hands across the keyboard.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: But there are certain keys that lay in a position for the fingering of certain instruments that's better, also for the voice. For instance a tenor saxophone seems to be closer to the human voice of the average man's voice, you know.
And the baritone has a rather base sound, you know. So all right, so there's a certain clef, a certain place --

A range, you see, for each instrument. Now, also the fingering. There are certain places that it's easier to finger, manipulate the fingers. Of course the pianist, he must have fingers, nimble fingers, and he must be able to do things that other people can't do, because he has to use both hands all over the key board. And you know, the other instruments like the saxophone, they have a special place to put their fingers, in a certain area, and then they change positions, they change registers. Then they can press down on a key which will change the register --
-- and they just continue fingering in the same place.
They don't have to move their hands.
See, but a pianist must go up and down the piano, you know, and he has many more notes to read, which is very complicated.
